extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students learning hygiene, public health, and nutrition
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on selecting, preparing, and consuming foods and beverages for health: includes criteria for judging animal meat and slaughter-houses, principles of digestion and cooking, balanced rations, and advice on water, condiments, and stimulants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of animals for food (health and condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two points to be noted in an animal about to be killed, namely, whether the animal is healthy, that is, free from disease,--and whether it is in proper condition, neither too young nor too old, is well-grown and well-nourished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject flesh of any animal apparently suffering from disease; prefer animals that move freely, have bright eyes, moist nostrils, clear skin, unhurried respiration, tranquil circulation, good appetite, and (if ruminant) chew the cud when at rest. Avoid emaciated animals; prefer proper weight with adequate fat and firm elastic flesh and supple skin. Beware of bob-veal (calves under three weeks); calf should be at least three weeks old to be fit for food.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorize animal diseases by risk (transmissible vs spoilage/toxicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the diseases to which animals are subject, some are objectionable because of the possibility of the direct transmission of their disease to those eating the flesh, while others are objectionable because the flesh is spoiled and so causes irritation in the stomach and intestines of those eating it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of transmissible diseases: trichinosis, tuberculosis, measles of pigs. Examples of diseases causing toxic spoilage: epidemic pneumonia, foot-and-mouth disease, Texas fever, anthrax, hog cholera. Do not use meat from animals with either class of disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognizing an unhealthy animal (observable signs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The unhealthy animal can usually be recognized by a casual examination ... characterized by such an examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signs of sickness include rough or standing coat, dry or foaming nostrils, heavy eyes, protruding tongue, difficult respiration, slow/uncertain movement, and abnormal organ function. Healthy signs include free movement, bright eye, moist nostril, clear skin, unhurried respiration, no unpleasant breath odor, tranquil circulation, good appetite, and normal thirst.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tuberculosis in carcasses — regulated exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: "All carcasses affected with tuberculosis and showing emaciation shall be condemned. All other carcasses affected with tuberculosis shall be condemned, except those in which the lesions are slight, calcified, or encapsulated, and are confined to certain tissues ... and excepting also those which may ... be rendered into lard or tallow."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carcasses with slight, localized, calcified or encapsulated lesions confined to certain tissues may be used after cutting out lesions; where lesions affect more than one or two parts the carcass must be rendered at not less than 220°F for four hours into lard or tallow. The tuberculin test may condemn milk cows even with slight lesions, but permissible use of carcass parts is allowed where lesions are segregated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule against using animals dying of disease
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, it should be remembered that any animals dying of diseases are not fit for food, and this applies to all animals, from the largest to the smallest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminate animals dying a natural death or out of condition; animals dying by accident may be exceptions but diseased carcasses should not be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slaughter-house sanitation standards
rubrics_metrics.description: There is ... the further question of the sanitary condition of the slaughter-house and the care of the meat after being dressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slaughter-houses should be kept clean: ceilings, walls, partitions frequently painted or scrubbed; floors water-tight with proper drains so blood does not saturate wood; abundant clean water for washing; complete ventilation; provision for lifting and moving carcasses without handling. Avoid premises infested with flies, insects, rats, and strong effluvia; such conditions promote putrefactive bacteria and contamination by flies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refuse handling and prohibition on feeding entrails to hogs
rubrics_metrics.description: The obnoxious practice prevails of maintaining a herd of swine to consume the entrails of the slaughtered animals ... Such hog meat is not fit for food.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refuse from the slaughter-house ought to be carried away and buried (or used in gardens) rather than left for hogs; prompt removal of refuse improves the establishment's sanitary character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooking destroys parasites and micro-organisms (importance of thorough cooking)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is reason to be more certain in sanitary science than that the application of heat destroys animal parasites and micro-organisms ... there is comparatively little real danger in eating diseased meat when cooked, ... the fearful ravages of bad ham have been largely due to occasions where the ham has been eaten raw or semi-raw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thorough cooking prevents transmission of many parasites (e.g., trichinae) and microorganisms; avoid eating raw or underdone pork or other meats where parasites are possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trichinosis transmission and prevention
rubrics_metrics.description: The most common example of the direct transmission of disease from animals to men is through the development of the parasite in a pig, known as 'trichinosis.' ... the means of prevention is very simple and implies merely the thorough cooking of the meat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trichinae may be numerous yet invisible in pork; after ingestion of raw/undercooked pork the worms reproduce massively in humans. Prevention: avoid eating raw or underdone swine flesh in any variety; cook thoroughly to destroy trichinae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digestive-process principle: mastication (chewing) and saliva
rubrics_metrics.description: The mouth plays the first part ... two operations are performed. First the food is crushed and ground by the teeth ... The other function of the mouth is to mix with the food the saliva ... The action of the saliva on starch is to convert it into sugar, which is easily absorbed later on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thorough chewing is essential, especially for starchy foods (saliva acts on starch). Neglect of chewing can overburden subsequent digestive organs. Horace Fletcher advocated many chews per mouthful; avoid swallowing without chewing (e.g., hurried bread and milk).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence and roles of digestive juices (stomach, pancreas, bile)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the stomach ... gastric juice acts on proteids. ... At the beginning of the smaller intestine the juices from the pancreas are added ... From this gland comes a material which can act on all kinds of food ... When thoroughly mixed with the bile and pancreatic juice, the contents of the intestine are gradually absorbed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide foods suited to each organ's function; avoid overloading any single digestive organ. Proper cooking and mastication aid the stomach and subsequent pancreatic/biliary digestion and absorption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced rations and food classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists have divided all food into four classes, namely, proteids, carbohydrates, fats, and inorganic salts ... proteids are particularly useful in building up cell tissue, carbohydrates in providing for muscular energy, fats in keeping up the normal warmth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-designed ration provides proper amounts adjusted to occupation and digestive ability. A commonly assumed proportion is proteids:carbohydrates ≈ 1:4. Use tables (Atwater, Chittenden, etc.) to compute daily needs by age, sex, and activity; combine foods (bread+cheese, bread+butter, potatoes+meat) to achieve balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use food composition tables to plan diets
rubrics_metrics.description: The following table ... gives the percentage composition of some of the more common foods: (bread, flour, oatmeal, rice, peas, potatoes, milk, cheese, meats, eggs, butter, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to composition tables to calculate how much of each food is needed to meet proteid, carbohydrate and fat requirements (example: man moderate work requires 4.1 oz proteids and 17.5 oz carbohydrates; combinations of bread, potatoes, and meat reduce required weight of single items).

rubrics_metrics.name: Food combinations to achieve nutritive balance
rubrics_metrics.description: It is curious ... one naturally combines different articles of food, so as to make up the well-balanced daily ration ... Bread and cheese are well known to make up a good combination ... Eggs alone are a very poor article of diet since no starch at all is present ... Milk and bread is more palatable as well as more nutritious than milk alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine foods that complement each other's deficiencies (e.g., starch + proteid + fat) to make palatable, balanced meals; ensure starch is paired with proteid/fat when needed (eggs need cereal/bread).

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect and manage human appetite and variety
rubrics_metrics.description: One other factor needs to be considered ... the respect which must be paid to the appetite. The most carefully balanced ration will fail to satisfy ... unless it is served attractively and unless sufficient variety is provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide attractive presentation and variety; monotony reduces appetite and may impair digestion (e.g., continuous salty food leads to scurvy). Appetite generally is a safe guide to quantity and quality but is unreliable under poor health, lack of exercise, poor housing, or stimulant use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooking methods and their digestive effects (avoid frying)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good cooking is as important ... Cooking may be said to be the first step ... A great deal is said nowadays about overeating ... No discussion on foods would be complete without a repetition of the frequently given warning, against fried meats and vegetables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer roasting, stewing, boiling or baking to frying. Frying coats food with fat difficult for digestive juices to penetrate; unless thoroughly chewed and fried in very hot fat, fried food may pass through the stomach undigested. Proper cooking softens tissues to aid digestion; overcooking can harden fibers and impede digestion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and physical state around meals (exercise, rest, exhaustion)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the individual is exhausted or even tired, no complete digestion is possible ... In hot weather, a heavy meal should not be eaten until after a half hour's rest and after copious water drinking ... After meals, violent exercise is not desirable ... moderate exercise after ordinary meals is not objectionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid heavy/vigorous exercise immediately after meals; rest briefly before eating when exhausted or overheated; moderate post-meal activity is acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychic factors: smell, attention, and enjoyment aiding digestion
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies ... have shown that the smell of food, or the mere suggestion of food, stimulates the organs for the production of the digestive juices ... It follows, then, that the enjoyment of food is quite as important as any other digestive function ... eating with no interest or attention is the best way to induce subsequent indigestion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present food attractively, encourage pleasant anticipation and attention at meals (cheerful intercourse), and avoid hurried, inattentive eating (e.g., quick-lunch counter) to promote proper secretion of digestive juices and better digestion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water consumption guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary person ought to drink, or consume with his food in some way, at least two quarts of water a day ... the contention that water should not be taken at meals is not particularly tenable except as the continual swallowing of water increases the tendency to swallow food without chewing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consume about two quarts of water daily to maintain bodily fluids and aid organ function; drinking during or after meals is acceptable and may aid dilution and absorption, but avoid excessive sipping that encourages swallowing without chewing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and cautious use of condiments, coffee, and tea
rubrics_metrics.description: Chief among these are the condiments and drinks, particularly coffee and tea. So far as the nutritive value ... goes, they are practically negligible, and yet, undoubtedly, these flavors play an important part in the suggestion of pleasure ... Coffee and tea are generally consumed merely for the pleasure ... Both, however, have a certain stimulating effect on the nervous system ... the exhilarating effect can be produced only at the expense of nerves and muscular tissue which must be later atoned for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use condiments to aid appetite and enjoyment but not as nutritional substitutes. Provide salt as needed (body craves salt). Limit use of strong tea/coffee; avoid relying on stimulants in lieu of food—they can deplete nerve and muscular resources if used to suppress appetite for food.
